articles.summary: Something strange just popped up in the Gulf of Mexico: a hurricane. Well, not so much Hurricane Isaias, which strengthened into a Category 3 before its predicted landfall along the Florida Panhandle late Friday. It’s more the timing of it: This is the first Atlantic hurricane of the season, which began all the way back in June. That smashes the previous record in the satellite era for the latest first hurricane of a season, September 11. “This is pretty astounding, really, to break a record by just about a month,” said Brian McNoldy, a senior research associate who studies hurricanes at the University of Miami. So what’s with the extraordinary delay? El Niño, of all things . Even though that band of warm water is on the other side of the Americas in the Pacific, it messes with two of the fundamental ingredients for making hurricanes in the Atlantic: wind and humidity. To spawn a tropical cyclone, you need warm water, which provides energy, as well as high humidity and winds moving in a consistent direction. articles.title: Germany raises growth forecast in spite of Iran war concerns
articles.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
articles.summary: Germany, Europe’s biggest economy, raised its growth forecast, a rare bright spot as regional economic worries abound. Berlin anticipates GDP will expand by 1.3% this year and a similar rate in 2027 — lackluster by global standards, but nonetheless significantly up from previous estimates , with the Iran war taking less of a toll than expected. Elsewhere in the EU, the news was less upbeat: France’s 10-year bond yields climbed to highs not seen in decades , raising worries that Paris “may have crossed the line from too big to fail to too big to save, ” the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote. Political uncertainty pushed the euro toward its fifth weekly fall , capping a dismal run for European financial markets. — Jeronimo Gonzalez
